entries.previousTitle: Loss Aversion – when losing hurts more than winning feels good
entries.title: Loss Aversion – when a loss can carry more weight than an equivalent gain
entries.description:
Loss Aversion is the idea that, relative to a reference point, a loss can receive more subjective weight than an equivalent gain. It is an important part of prospect theory, but it should not be treated as a universal rule or as a fixed claim that every loss always counts twice as much as a gain.

Where can it show up?
- Risk choices: losing 100 can feel more important than an otherwise comparable chance to gain 100.
- Product and policy decisions: the same change can look different depending on whether it is presented as giving up something already expected or gaining something new.
- Project reviews: stopping can feel like accepting a loss, which can influence the decision even when future costs and benefits should be evaluated separately.

A better check
- State the reference point explicitly: what counts as a gain and what counts as a loss?
- Compare equal-sized positive and negative changes using the same probabilities and time horizon.
- Rewrite the decision in absolute outcomes when that is possible, not only as gains or losses from the current frame.
- Keep sunk costs separate from future value. A painful write-off is not automatically a reason to invest more.
- Do not apply one universal loss-aversion coefficient. Recent meta-analyses disagree substantially about the average size and robustness of the effect.
entries.reason: The legacy page treated Loss Aversion as a simple universal tendency and mixed it with examples better explained by sunk costs or disposition effects. Recent meta-analyses disagree substantially about the average magnitude and robustness of loss aversion, so the reviewed top copy keeps the reference point and evidence debate explicit.
